div.head: FARM OPERATIONS FOR SEPTEMBER.
div.p: FARM OPERATIONS FOR SEPTEMBER.
Harvest is still our principal work. - Wheat and bean carrying going on; rich cciverings also want at- tention. Bean carrying, elachlug, and thatching will be our last harvest work:—

When. the weather is flee, corn dries thickest in broad band or swathe. When corn is wet it should not be tied up. When-the weather is uncertain no corn should be allowed to remain down, but should be tied up as it is cut, and neatly stocked. Wheat and oats are usually tied into sheaves, while barley is more fre- quently carried loose. As to the advisability of this method of harvesting barley, much depends aeon the season and the locality. Fine seasons make slovenly harvesters, and hence we find less care taken both in hay and corn harvest in the aonth than in the north Of England. Oar north country friends would not think for a moment of carting their barley loose. as they know that they might easily get into a sad difficulty by so doing; but south of the Trent experience makes as bold. Loose barley, when well got, will come out from the stack a better and more uniform colour than that which was tied up. Mice cannot make way through a stack of loose barley any more than they can through a hay rick. Labour is also unquestionably saved, so that there is mirth to be said in layout' of loose carting for barley. Pea "wads" must be turned daily, or where the land is dry, once in two days; no crop suffers more quickly from rain, the haulm goon losing quail y_ as fodder when exposed to wet. Therefore peas should be carted as soon as they are ready, and the rick should be thatched immediately. A well topped up wheat rick will stand a good deal of rain, but a pea stack will wet through from top to bottom in a wonderfully short time.

This month we must be industrious with our horses too, preparing land for wheat planting. Summer !al- lows should be landed up, if not already done. Pea brush ploughed, scud, and harrowed, twitch got off, and again ploughed ready for seed. Beans and clover brash should also be ploughed, if time can be spared; if not, time must be found next month.

Plough a few acres of last year's wheat ground, and plant for early vetches; in fact, by the latter end of the month it will be time for the main crop. Also rya and vetches, or rye alone. A good arrangement in rotation for spring food for horses or sheep is—first plant some rye, which of course Comes in early • then mix the seed; patting in half vetches and half rye; and for the last crop, all vetches By doing so we are enabled to cut early, and have a continuation. If trifolium, is planted, put it on wheat brush, just harrowing or scuffling it in. The seed requires but little covering, but must not be-attempted on clay.

Stora sheep and lambs, also cow stock, will do well on wheat and bean stubbles as soon as the crop is re- moved. The keep is valaable, as stock do well upon it for a change, besides clearing up the rubbish, and giving the old pasture land a rest. Any calves under twelve months old should now be housed at night, as they are vety susceptible of cold. Late turnips, or rather whits turnips, may require a little looking to as regards weeding. All ploughs, 800138' harrows, and drills should be put in order this month for wheat planting.—Far tners' Herald.

SALMON FISHERIES AND THE NEW ACT. 'The new act lately passed relatiug to salmon fisheries in Eagland and Wales came into operation on Friday. A GIRL BURIED ALIVE.

Mr. Driffisld, coroner, held an inquest at the Wheat Sheaf Inn, Orford-lane, on Monday, on the body of Ellen Slater, twelve years of age, daughter of Richard Slater, a railway labourer, resi ling in Jockey-lane.— Thomas Buttress, 16, Angel-yard, stated that on Saturday afternoon last, shortly after t .elye o'clock, he was passing down Lythgee's-lane, when he met a woman who informed him that a little lad was being smothered in a "sandhols." He went to the place— ome 200 yards away frJna where he was—and found that a little boy was buried in the sand up to his neck. He at once liberated him. Near to him was a spade which he commenced to dig out of the sand with his hands, when his fingers came in contact with a por- tion of the body of the deceased girl, which he subse- quently extricated. Life however was extinct. He be- lieved the children had gone to the place for sand to pat on the house fl 3or. The land on which the sand was lying belonge i to the Cheshire Li ei Cocimittee.— The father of the deceased stated that on Saturday] last, deceased had gone to the heap for some sand to put on the house floor, and he had frequently forbidden his children to do this.—Joseph Worsley, a boy a,-)ont ten years of age, stated that he and the deeeased were getting sand on the day in question, when the top fell in, burying deceased and himself up to the necic. Re - did not know what the deceased wanted sand for, but he wanted it to sell.—An Impector of the Permanent Way, in the service of the Cheshire Lines Committee was present, and was asked by the Coroner if he had not better take steps to stop children going to the sand heap in future.—The Inspector. I cannot say, sir.— The Coroner: You must not let chit iren go there to get smothered.—The Inspector We cannot help them trespassing.—The Coroner : You must represent it to the directors. div.head: BRITISH ASSOCIATION.
div.p: THE BRITISH ASSOCIATION.

The opening address to the British Association was delivered on Wednesday, at Glasgow, by Dr. Andrews, the president. The address was a review of the principal scientific features of the year, and in con- cluding it'Dr. Andrews remarked that the progress of mankind would be marked by alternate periods of ac- tivity and repose, and would not be the work of any one nation or race; and he pointed out that the re- sources of nature were not confined to steam, nor to the combustion of coal.

div.p: BOARDS OF GUARDIANS AND SCHOOL FEES.

The Clerk to the Salford Board of Guardians has reminded the Board that by the new Education Act, which comes into force at the beginning of next years the school fees for the children of all parents who are unable to pay them shall be defrayed by the Gusxdians instead of by the School Board. The amount of fees paid by the School Board during the half-year ended Lady-day, 1876, was £621 Bs. 41. div.head: JURY LISTS.
div.p: THE JURY LISTS.

Next Sunday the lists of all persons in England liable to serve as jurymen will be exhibited on the church doors, and those who are sixty years of age and up- wards can claim exemption by applying to the Over- seers of their respective parishes. It is a mistaken notion that if summoned they can be excused on ac- count of their age, and judges have constantly to tell the applicants that until their names are removed from the lists they are bound to serve. There is a pro. vision in the new Poor Law Act by which the justices of counties can make an allowance to their clerks for their service in relation to the jury lists.

MR. GLADSTONE ON CURATES' STIPENDS. Mr. Gladstone, in reply to a Devonshire curate who appealed to him to lay before the public the pressing need of some authoritative and immediate steps being taken to increase the stipends of curates in the National Church, writes as follows "Dear Sir,—l am very sensible of the importance of the subject of your letter, but I do not quite under- stand what, in describing the efficiency of voluntary societies, you have its view as an effective means for improving the state of things. Something has already, beyond doubt, been effected by the working of" supply and demand," although this law has but a restricted action in regird to clerical remuneration. And more, I hope, may be effected, but clerical labour is likely to remain, on the average, the lowest paid with reference to its value.—Yours obediently and faithfully, "W. E. GLLASTONE."

A dispute between a Warrington master and his journeymen was lately reported in the Examiner, the grounds of which were that the men were sued in the County Court for damage done to a batch of bread alleged to have been spoiled through their negligence. The men's defence was that the inferior character of the flour and, berm, and the use of alum by their employer, was the real cause of the injury complained of. The case was adjourned at the time referred tor and came on for re-hearing at the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before Judge Ffoulkes. After the hearing of a mass of evidence on both sides the Judge in deliveiing judgment said ; In this case there are four actions all tried together. ' First, three actions for the amount of wages claimed by these men. The wages have been kept back by their employers, who claim a right to do so under a certain written agreement, which was said to have been read or shown them by Millington, the foreman, and agreed to by him personally, and sanctioned by them. The evidence upon that point was undoubtedly not very satisfactory. I don't think, however, that is a very materiql point, and I am still of the same opinion as when I read it, and that was with regard to the burning of the bread in future, in which case Messrs. As- suming the agreement was communicated to these four men and assented to by them, still I don't think that if it came under that head Messrs. Hallwood would be entitled to keep back the wages. They had . notice to go, and they worked the week out, and clearly earned their standing wages. The only difference is as to the overtime, which was not earned on the Monday, and there will be a deduction of Is. 3d. to each of them. IT is generally acknowledged that Elemen- tary Education is a more difficult task to undertake than education on secondary sub- jects. To teach the A B Cto a child is a greater achievment than to teach reading to a child who already knows his AB C. We have undertaken to instruct second child- hood in the political alphabet of its own times, and we confess that it would have been easier to us, had we spent our time in a less pedagogic fashion, it is difficult to realise the mental condition of a man, who, having m.staken his vocation, converts news- paper propr.etorship into the trade of a political huckster, and who, is not un- reasonably supposed to have contributed some of the dubious proceas to the endowment of Greenville University—an establishment which figures in prices cur- rent, and which appears to be a kind of shop where people pawn their ignorance, and get a ticket to certify it. That a man who has been meddling and muddling with news- papers for the last twenty years should never have heard of Catholic emanicipation, or Jewish Disabilities, would be surprising if we did not know that an exclusive aid de- vouring devotion to the more sordid side a the profession produces an inteliectuai paralysis which kills all intelligent or rational interest in public affairs—past or cur ant—no tvisibly rroductive of immediate pudding. But as we are assured that whilst there is life there is hope, we will not deem it wholly impossible that a ray of honest poli- tical light may reach the patient who com- plains that the Liberal party "might have done something to mitigate the sufferings of Dissenters, if so inclined." Sometimes a child propounds a question, unaware of its import yet which one elucidates for the sake of the bystanders, and we will proceed to take up the thread of our reply to the jour- nalistic enfant terrible- of the Warrington Guardian.

Soon after the Catholics had obtained jus- tice, and the friends of the Jews were •Itting forward their title to the same mea- re, L-71 John Russel and his followers su ..flution to the civil and turned their a..... religious disabilities uruL: which. these Dis- senters suffered, who, while bet:: akin to the State Church in matters of creed, were yet outside its communion. So recently as 1834 the three most interesting events in a man's life were civilly ignored, were, so to speak, illegal, if he and his representatives re/used to submit to certain laws imposed by the State Chuich. Unless, as a baby, he was baptised by a clergyman of the Church, there was no legal evidence of his existence; unless his marringe was solemnised at one of her altars, he was for ever afterwards breaking the seventh commandment; unless the Church of England service was read over his corpse, he was not buried, he was only interred. The Reformed Parliament undertook to alter this state of things. In 1836, Lord John Russell introduced and carried a measure for the registration of births, marriages, and deaths, and by it bap- tism and marriage, according to the ritual of the Church, were optional. But still a Dissenter could not be buried in the grave yard of his Parish Church, unless the clergyman was there to convert his corpse; and this objection was met by the Dissen- ters, by their providing themselves with cemetries so convenient, vast and beautiful, that now-a-days the Paiish Church yard is seldom preferred, even by Churchmen. And now an interval takes place, not in the energy and determination of John Bright's party to give civil equality to all, irrespective of creed, but in the actual re- dress of any of the remaining grievances which it had pledged itself to effect. Be- sides their exclusion from burial in church- yards, without the reading of the Church's ritual by the Church's minister, the only other burden of which Dissenters complained was the payment of Church rates. It is but fair to remark that the Church had been tolerant e-nough of the religious exemptions which the I)issenters had secured, but in the matter of burial and the payment of Churc rates her pocket was touched—for even the Church has a pocket. In the year 1839 Dissenters commenced refusing to pay Church rates, and many of them suffered distraint and imprisonment in consequence. We confess that we have an imperfect sym- pathy with this mode of resistance. To resist -a law- not always the right or the best way to repea; Laws should only be re- pealed by the same constlonsl. instru- ments with which they were enacted. Re- sides, in the present case, it is sometimes said in defence of the Church, that although the Dissenters urged conscientious objections against the payment of rates, on the other hand the Church might say that its build- ings were national property, that they were open to all, and that, moreover, the rate was chargeable on property and not on con- Sciences, and that therefore landlords would benefit by their abolition, and not tenants. In 1834 Earl Grey's ministry attempted to solve this question by substituting for the Church rates an annual grant from the con- solidated fund, but the Dissenters were acute enough to perceive that this was simply a compromise, and that they would be paying Church rates and calling it some- thing else. In 1837, Lord Melbourne tried to reconcile Churchmen and Dissenters by another scheme, but this time it was the Churchmen who repudiated the measure. A long and subtle contention now commenced In 1841 the first bill for the abolition of Church rates was hitt( duced, and was re- jected without a discussion, but from that year to the year 1863, when the bill was carried, John Bright's party, both in and out of the House, were unwearying alike in their patience and their energy; and at this day the only disability under which Dissenters suffer is, that they can- not be buried in churchyards with- out the sanction of the presiding parsou, but are driven to the refuge of pic- turesque cemeteries, where neither crescent, cross or wreath of violets, are prohibited. And now our task is ended. We have, for the time being, assumed the functions of a National School teacher of a paiticular section of English History: the work of John Bright's party in dealing with Dissent during the last fifty years. We have seen that during this period, Catholics, Jews, and the seceders from the State Church, have been grudgingly but effectually liberated from the social and political servitude under which they existed up to the year 1829. The bloodless revolutions of reason may take longer to bring about than the revolutions effected by the superior strength of numbers; but they are more lasting when they are ac- complished. Popular passions and popular ignorance are powerful impelling forces, but it is the happy mode of warfare, peculiar to intelligence and convic ion, to win by re- cruiting their smaller armies from the n )ble deserters from the ranks of prejudice and in- difference. And this is effected only by the strategy of unwearying patience, and the in- extinguishable enthusiasm of humanity. The triumphs of civil and religious freedom accomplished by ' 'John Bright and his party" are recognised by all classes of politicians in the land, and naturally, most of all, by that great party of Dissent to whose patriotism the country owes so much Plat has made its history noble. The miserable idolators of gain who fatten on a national prosperity which they have done nothing to create, and do nothing to maintain, are always with us. In that article we shall have something to say res- pecting that greatest of popular superstitions, the so-called " penny-a-liner," a "gentle- man of the press," for whom Mr. Mackie appears to entertain a curiously ignorant and incomprehensible antipathy.

OUR ponderous contemporary, gr. Mackie, omits no opportunity of exhibiting his ludi- crous and almost incredible unacquaintance with the profession into which "circum- stance, the unspiritual god and miscreator " —as Byron has it—has so curiously thrust him. In his issue of Saturday last there ap- peared an article in which he was good enough to take "Justice's justice" under his special protection, and to express his belief that it was often a much better thing than it was represented. To say that the spirit of evil, for instance, is not so black as he is painted, is merely to propound one of those imposing platitudes which make the liteatry capital of a small cl les of newspaper writers, and on which they imagine it is possibl6 to build a reputa- tion—which it undoubtedly does, of a kind. The occasion of Mr. Mackie's sagacious ob- servation seems to have been the passing, by some of our local:magistrates, of a somewhat lenient sentence on a man who was put into the dock for bursting one of his wife's eyes, and possibly of so endangering her other eye that th 4 unhappy creature might have been blinded for life. The gentlemen who tried the hideous ruffian whose crime—had it been committed in Bulgaria would have roused their honest indignation were in a merciful mood that morning, and, we suppose, yielding to the prayer of the mutilated and disfigured wife, com- passionately consented to inflict a nominal penalty and merely "bound him over." We humbly venture to think that the sentence in question was remarkable for its dispro- portionate lenity, and we can well believe that the magistrates who gave it would hesitate to make that particular sentence the prevail- ing standard of punishment for crimes of so barbarous a character. The sentence was probably one of' those judicial slips which happen occasionally not merely to gentlemen in the commission of the peace, but also—if less frequently—to stipendiary magistrates and the judges of the land. They are not, however, in our opinion, the less to be re- gretted, and no gentleman' whatever may be his social elevation, cin be the worse, or the worse humoured, for being now and then reminded that he is human. Many years have passed since the heart of the English nation has been so moved and thrilled as it is now being moved and thrilled by a great horror or an enormous political excitement. The indescribable barbarities perpetrated by the Turkish troops in Bulgaria, and the revelations of the inhuman character of Turkish misrule, exercised over its Christian provinces, seems to have effected a sudden and terrible revolution in the mind and heart of England with regard to the permanence of Turkish dominion in Europe. It is scarcely too much to say that the tem- pest of astonishment and indignation conse- quent on the horrible revelations of the Daily News commissioner with respect to the scenes of blood and outrage that have lately occurred in Bulgaria signalises a revolu ion in the public sentiment of England towards the Ottoman Government. and a mighty change in the general policy of the Powers of Europe towards it. Every day the daily newspapers abound with reports of public meetings held in the most considerable towns and cities of the kingdom at which the leaders of local opinion, almost itrespec- tive of party, assemble to denounce the mas- sacres and violations in Bulgaria, and to urge on the British Government the imme- diate duty of publicly freeing it- self from every possible suspicion of complicity with a power which has outraged every practice and principle of modern civilisation. It would be impossible in such space as we can command to do more than briefly indicate the character of the great storm which is convulsing the moral nature of 1 ngland on this terrible Eastern question. Lt a great meeting at Halifax on Friday, Mr. John Crossley, M.P. presid- ing, Mr. Stansfeld expressed the feel- ings which animated that portion of Yorkshire. He deprecated, as he had a righ ; to do, everything of • the character of political partisanship and ap- peared there only to declare the deep sense of shame ;of sickening shuddering horror with which he had rea 1 the details of the atrocities so calculated to haunt and har- row the human imagination. Mr. Stansfeld declared that whatever Government might I be in power, and whether it might be will- ing or unwilling, the frightful story from the East was destined to mould the future foreign policy of England. These sentiments were received with unanimous sympathy. Similar declarations have been made all over the country, and memorials in accord- ance with such views have been forwarded to the Ii nglish Government. The ministers of religion of varying creeds are also lifting up their voices against Turkish barbarities. Dean Stanley, speaking on Sunday, depre- cated all party watchwords in this terrible matter. lie declared that , "It was our mission in the path of duty to repress and punish and prevent such horrors. The solution of the great problem which ,attached to the settling of the rights and claims of the various races and creeds in Europe and in Asia was a task too lofty and too serious to become the monopoly of any one party or hection, either in the Church or ia the State. It was a duty and a task which belonged to our common patriotism and our common Christianity, and to Statesmen and citizens on both sides of the State."

Mr. Spurgeon, on the same day, offered up a special prayer, " beseeching (31-Id to cause the Turks to be defeated for the atrocities they had committed upon Christian women and children; and he also prayed that they might soon be driven out of Europe, and the whole of the Mahammedah power swept away from off the face of the earth." The prayer was delivered in a most impressive manner, and the tone in which the "Amen" was spoken at its close clearly indicated that the wish expressed by Vie Speaker, was entirely in consonance with the sentiments of his vast congre- gation.

Bishop Fraser, in letters to the Tinles and to chairmen of public meetings to which ho has been invited, expresses with character- istic fervour the opinions which everywhere prevail. The Bishop declares that

"It is no mere question of the exigency of a ministry or of the fate of a government, or of a line of ordinary policy which might be safely left to the hands that are used to pilot the vesiel of the State. Tt is a question concerning, and deeply concerning, tho honour and character for humanity of the people of England; and it would seem as though the people of England, if they would have their honour and character for humanity safe, must take them Into their own keep- ing."

Mr. John Bright, who understands pro- bably better than any other public man in the Empire that fatal Eastern question which has so long been the bane of English politics has illuminated the national debate —or rather expressed the profound senti- ment which isinow pulsing over the land, in a letter which will be memorable as the most formidable impeachment of our Eastern diplomacy.
LETTER FROM MR. JOHN BRIGHT

A crowded and enthusiastic meeting was held at Rochdale under the presidency of the Mayor on Mon- day night, at which letters were read from Mr. John Bright, the Bishop of Manchester, and Mr. J. B. Potter, member for the borough. Resolutions expres- sive ot abhorrence of the Turkish barbarities in Bul- garia were passed. The following is Mr. Bright'B letter : Inverinate House, Lochal eh, Scotland, Sept. let., 1876.

Dear Sir,—Your letter has just reached me late this evening. I have no time to write anything for the meeting. The question is one not to be treated hastily and I almost fear to say anything about it. More than 20 years ago I explained my views of the Eastern or Turkish difficulty. The Government of the day dif - eared from me, as did the vast majority of the nation, 'nd the war with Russia was entered upon. Some of it, results we now know. It is said to have cost Eng- land 40,000 lives and £100,000,000 of money. It cost all the parties to the war more than half a million of Jives. Since then it has ccst us ten millions a year in increased military expenses, or £200,000,000 in all, and in loans to the Turkish Sultan it has probably cost England another hundred millions sterling. The money aocount thus comes to four hundred million, (4400,000,000) sterling; the loss of life was enormous. The policy of that day was popnlar, and the result is what I have described. I was assailed and insulted in and by almost all the newspapers in the kingdom, because I condemned the war and the polioy which led to it. The present Government accepts the policy of the G wernment of 1854. It is now understood throughout the world to be the main if not the one supporter of the Turkish rule in Europe. If it had acted with Russia and the other Powers, it is almost certain the Servian war would net have taken place, and but for the confidence caused by the support of England, the Turks would not have dared to have committed the horrid crimes of which they have been guilty in Bulgaria. In these crimes there is nothing new. They are familiar to all who know anything of the Turkish history. What is new is that the English Government cannot see the crimes till an English newspaper describes and de- nouncesthem and that an English Minister, speaking for himself and Zia colleagues, treats them as of small account, and as the common incidents of insurrection and of war. lam not sure that a Minister truly re- presenting English feeling would not have withdrarn the Queen's Ambassador from Constantinople, and have refused longer to receive a Minister from Turkey at the Queen's Court. The Government of England should clear itself of all partnership in the interest and the policy of the Turkish Government. It is a part- nership in no degree necessary to our interests, and degrades us in the estimation of every Christian nation. Every town oh oul 1 have its meeting, and protest &gait., st our country being stained and dis- graced by a participation in the policy and crimes of the Ttukish Government. Ido not think this can reach you before your meeting is held, but it is some relief to have written it.—l am, very truly yours, JOHN BRIGHT, To Mr, R. Hope Brown, Rochdale.

Mr. Gladstone, in a pamphlot just issued, and which in various forms is already in the hands of the people of England, has lighted up and exalted this great question with the large intelligence and the heroic and con- ocientious spirit which has made him one of tinmoit tlosted, hf if OW of tho
" servants of the State." Briefly Mr, Gladstone says : MR. GLADSTONE'S PAMPHLET.

Mr. Gladstone'e pamphlet on the "Bulgarian Horrors," was issued on Wednesday, and lengthy ex- t rads from it will be found in another page. The pamphlet is divided in seven parts :—(l) How the present Situation has been Brought About ; (2) Sketch of the Turkish Race and Government; (3) The Policy of the British Ministry; (4) The Questions and Answers; (5) The Discovery of the Bulgarian Horrors, (6) The British Fleet at Besika Bay; (7) The Snares to be Avoided; (8) The Ends to be Pursued. Mr. Gladstone attributes the present situation to the just confidence reposed in the Government of the day, of which it availed itself to the uttermost in adjourning discussion to the dying hours of the session, and al- lowing information to be obtained only by degrees from private and voluntary exertion. Mr. Gladstone approves of sending a naval force to Besika Bay, but thinks the wrong kind of force was sent, and that it was too obviously one meant to defy a foreign power, instead of being one to aid the Chi isti ans in the event of their being attacked. He condemns the talk about the restoration of our "prestige," that being, as he says the bane of all upiight politics. He rejoices that the working classes of this country have taken the lead in denouncing the horrible atrocities in Bulgaria, The Turks he describes as "the one great anti-human specimen of humanity." They "represent everywhere government by fore° as opposed to government by law• For the guide of this life they have a relentless fatalism; for its reward hereafter, a sensual paradise." Of the Russians Mr. Gladstone speaks with respect Hs writes, "I Bay the time is come for us to emulate Russia by sharing in her good deeds and to reserve our opposition until she shall visibly endeavour to turn them to evil ,account." He is anxious that the present strong flow of British feeling shall not be diverted into a wrong channel ' • and he advisee that his fellow-countrymen shall demand not the disin- tegration of Turkey on the one hand, nor the statui quo on the other, but the maintenance of the Turkish sovereignty, together with autonomy for the Christian provinces—Bosnia, Bulgaria, and Hel zegovina—just , as Servia and Roumania have enj eyed. He pleads, also, that indignation shall not be allowed to evaporate in words, but that active aid as well as passive sympathy shall be forthcoming ; and he especially commends to their support Lady Strangford'e mission. With regard to Mr. I3ourke's letter, the ex-Premier says that indig- na-ion is froth unless it leads to action. "The only two things that are worth saying the Under Secretary does not say. The first of them would have been that, until these horrible outrages are redressed and their authors punished, the British GleverLment would withdraw from Turkey the moral and even material support we have been lending her against Europe. The other was, that after crimes of so vast a scale and so deep a dye the British Government would no longer be a party o the maintenanui of Turkish administra- tion in Bulgaria. It is, then, the negative part of this letter that signifies. Mr. Bourke's words, viewing their date, are futile. But his silence is trump et- tongued ; it proclaims that even last week, on the 27th of August, the Government were still unconverted; and, warning us what we have to expect, Mr. Gladstone spurs the people of England onwards in the movement which is to redeem its compromised and endangered honour."
MR. GLADSTONE AND HIS CONSTITUENTS.
At a meeting of the council of the Greenwich Liberal Association, on Wednesday night, the following letter from Mr. Gladstone was read :
University Club, 6th September, 1876.

Dear Sir,—l have rcceived your letter, and will re- main in the South for ttie meeting on or as late as Saturday. Should you wish to see me about the ar- rangements, I will keep any appointment at 73, Harley-street, or 18, CarUm House Terraae. If early in the day the better, and rather more convenient. The meeting will, I hope, be addreesed by others besides myself, and in my opinion it would be advisable to move an address to the Crown praying for the objects which it may think ought to be sought for.
Your faithful and obedient servant, (Signed) W. E. GLLDsTorns.
To Mr. E. Davis.
It was resolved by the council that Mr. Gladstone be invited to come and address his constituents at Blackheath next Saturday a f ternoon, at three o'clock. „

In the meantime the country seems, as it were, moving in the light of beacon fires' extending to every point of the compass. Mr. Gladstone is to address, immediately, a great meeting at Blackheath—a meeting representing not a party but the nation. This contagion of public spirit will probably leave no corner of England wholly un- affected by its force, and there are visible abroad all the signs of a great and porten- tous crisis—a beneficient crisis there is ground to hope—in the territorial and poli- tical position of Turkey and of Europe.
